clue.text: What contentious folk often get for seconds?

definitions.meaning: quarrelsome people get their ..., meaning they become annoyed and defensive
to second a proposal is to support it, or back it up

explanation.surface: A question about what argumentative types are given when they ask for a second helping.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Seconds' looks like extra food or a measure of time; here it is the verb, as when one seconds a motion in a meeting.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are idioms: getting one's dander raised, and lending support to someone.

clue.text: British state's contribution to continental breakfast?

parts.note: to state is to utter; the 's is the link word is

explanation.surface: Britain's offering to a European morning meal.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the definition as an example: a continental breakfast is bread or croissants with this spread.
explanation.definitionFit: A spread on croissants and rolls forms part of the light European morning meal.

clue.text: Minister's canny, calling in the artillery

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is simply a minister

indicators.note: calling in means bringing something inside, so one word goes within the other

parts.note: cute means shrewd or canny
RA is the Royal Artillery

explanation.surface: A shrewd politician calls up the gunners.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Minister' suggests a politician; here it is a clergyman.
explanation.definitionFit: An assistant parish priest is a minister of religion.

clue.text: Music from Southern religious ceremonies?

parts.note: pi is slang for pious or religious
rituals are ceremonies

explanation.surface: Songs drawn from church services in the American South.
explanation.definitionFit: Spirituals are a genre of religious folk songs from African-American tradition.

clue.text: Here we go for relief — relief coming up in stages

parts.note: a po is a chamber pot, where one goes to relieve oneself

indicators.note: in a down clue coming up means the word is read from bottom to top, backwards

parts.note: aid means relief or help

explanation.surface: Charity relief arrives in phases.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Relief' is used twice: the first time bodily, for a chamber pot (PO), then as AID.
explanation.definitionFit: Podiums are raised platforms or stages for speakers and performers.

clue.text: Miserly investment in worthy sculpture, for instance

indicators.note: an investment puts something inside, so one word's letters are placed within the other

parts.note: fit means worthy, as in fit for a king
near is an old word for stingy or miserly

explanation.surface: A tight-fisted buyer puts money into a deserving statue.
explanation.definitionFit: Sculpture is one example of the visual arts made for beauty rather than use.

clue.text: Barrage's fluid seal broken

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is simply a barrage

indicators.note: broken means the letters are shattered and reassembled in another order

explanation.surface: A dam's watertight seal has failed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Barrage' looks like a dam; 'broken' shuffles FLUID and SEAL.
explanation.definitionFit: A volley of continuous gunfire is a barrage.

clue.text: Gas, once found, regularly discharged

indicators.note: regularly discharged means every other letter is thrown out, keeping the rest

explanation.surface: A gas leak, once discovered, kept being released.
explanation.definitionFit: A noble gas element, used in glowing signs.

clue.text: A game soldier first to attempt a written defence

parts.note: polo is a game played on horseback
GI is an American soldier

indicators.note: first to means only the opening letter of the next word is used

explanation.surface: A plucky soldier is first to try writing a justification.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Game' looks like an adjective, meaning plucky; it is the sport.
explanation.definitionFit: A formal written justification of one's opinions or conduct.

clue.text: Cow with last of clover to chew coming in later

indicators.note: coming in means these letters enter the word for later

parts.note: then means at a later time

indicators.note: last of means only the final letter of the word is used

parts.note: to eat is to chew food

explanation.surface: A cow chews clover, finishing the job later.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Cow' looks like the animal in this grazing scene, but it is a verb meaning intimidate.
explanation.definitionFit: To cow is to intimidate, which is what menacing someone does.

clue.text: Is rubbish put back in trunks?

indicators.note: put back tells the solver to read these joined words from the end to the start

parts.note: rot means nonsense or rubbish

explanation.surface: A query about whether garbage gets stowed back inside storage chests.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Trunks' suggests luggage or swimwear; here it means human torsos, the bodies without head and limbs.
explanation.definitionFit: Torsos are the trunks of the body, a plural Latin-style form of the anatomical word.

clue.text: Get dirty, menacing look after party

indicators.note: after places the menacing look behind the party in the finished word

parts.note: a disco is a dance party
to lour (or lower) is to frown or look threatening

explanation.surface: Someone gets grubby after scowling at a party.
explanation.definitionFit: To discolour is to stain or change colour, so to become soiled or dirty.

clue.text: "Almost clean" Brexit arranged, that can be delivered

indicators.note: arranged means the gathered letters are put into a new order
almost means the word clean is used without its final letter

explanation.surface: A political quip about a nearly tidy Brexit deal being organised and deliverable.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Almost' trims CLEAN to CLEA; 'arranged' shuffles CLEA with BREXIT.
explanation.definitionFit: Something extricable can be freed or released from a tangle, so rescued or delivered.

clue.text: Painter's energy always returns

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the definition is simply a painter

parts.note: go means energy or vigour

indicators.note: returns means the word for always is turned round to read backwards

parts.note: ay (or aye) is an old word for always or ever

explanation.surface: An artist's drive keeps coming back.
explanation.walkthrough: The poetic or dialect word for 'always' is the one needed here, not 'ever'.
explanation.definitionFit: Francisco de Goya was the great Spanish painter of the late 18th and early 19th centuries.

clue.text: Any child is mad giving pound for a necklace

indicators.note: mad means the letters go crazy into a new arrangement
giving pound for a means the letter for a pound is replaced by the letter a

parts.note: L is the abbreviation for a pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A crazed child trades a pound for a piece of jewellery.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Mad' shuffles ANY CHILD IS; then the L is swapped for A ('giving pound for a').
explanation.definitionFit: A string of flowers linked by their stems, worn round the neck by children.

clue.text: Wild animal with truer colour

indicators.note: wild suggests the letters run riot into a new order

explanation.surface: A feral creature is somehow a more faithful shade.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Wild' shuffles ANIMAL with TRUER.
explanation.definitionFit: Ultramarine is a deep blue pigment, a particular shade.

clue.text: Characteristic craft revolutionised nameless country

indicators.note: revolutionised means turned round, so the word reads backwards

parts.note: art means craft or skill

indicators.note: nameless means the abbreviation for name, N, is removed

parts.note: Denmark is a country

explanation.surface: A boat overturned an unnamed country's traditions.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Craft' looks like a boat; it is ART, reversed. Removing N from DENMARK leaves DEMARK.
explanation.definitionFit: A distinctive feature or habit is a hallmark or signature of someone.

clue.text: Charming qualities masking Nutmeg's ugly looks

indicators.note: masking means one word hides another inside it

parts.note: graces are charming qualities
Nutmeg is the setter, so Nutmeg's means I'm

explanation.surface: The setter's charm hides the faces being pulled.
explanation.walkthrough: A setter naming themself means I or ME; here 'Nutmeg's' is I'M.
explanation.definitionFit: Distorted facial expressions of pain or disgust are ugly looks.

clue.text: In Montmartre, a joint seldom found

parts.note: in Paris (Montmartre), the word for a is un in French
common means joint, shared

explanation.surface: A Paris spot where a cannabis cigarette is rare.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Joint' suggests a reefer or a pub; here it means shared.
explanation.definitionFit: Something rare is seldom found.

clue.text: Rein in twins, those running the enterprise

indicators.note: in places the word for rein inside the word for twins

parts.note: ringers are lookalikes, people dead ringers for each other
a lead is a rein or leash

explanation.surface: A parent restrains a pair of twins, or managers keep a business going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Twins' gives RINGERS, as in 'dead ringers', lookalikes.
explanation.definitionFit: Ringleaders head a group or scheme, usually a mischievous one, so they run it.

clue.text: Put paid to king, moving bishop not pawn

parts.note: K is the chess abbreviation for king

indicators.note: moving means the remaining letters are shifted into a new order
not means the pawn is left out of the word

parts.note: P is the chess abbreviation for pawn

explanation.surface: A chess game ended for a king when a bishop moved instead of a pawn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Moving' rearranges BISHO (bishop with P removed by 'not').
explanation.definitionFit: To put the lid on, or end, something; an informal verb for stopping a plan dead.

clue.text: Top husband in contest getting promotion

indicators.note: in places the abbreviation for husband inside the word for contest

parts.note: a bee is a contest, as in a spelling bee
an ad is a promotion or advertisement

explanation.surface: A top husband wins a contest and gets promoted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Top' looks like an adjective; it is slang for the verb kill, especially decapitate.
explanation.definitionFit: To top someone is slang for killing them, here by cutting off the head.

clue.text: What Jersey did, presumably, banning English humour

indicators.note: banning means a letter is excluded from the word

parts.note: a Jersey is a breed of cow, which would have mooed

explanation.surface: An island excluded English humour, or so one assumes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jersey' looks like the Channel Island, but it is the breed of dairy cow.
explanation.definitionFit: Humour in the sense of temper or frame of mind, as in 'in a good humour'.

clue.text: Whistleblower runs, busy and able to change direction

parts.note: a ref (referee) blows a whistle in football
R is the cricket abbreviation for runs
active means busy

explanation.surface: An informant flees, busy and nimble enough to switch course.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Whistleblower' suggests a leaker of secrets; here it is the referee.
explanation.definitionFit: A refractive medium bends light, changing the direction of its rays.

clue.text: Punster's last to cut gag

indicators.note: last means only the final letter of the punster is taken

parts.note: to etch is to cut a design into a surface

explanation.surface: The comedian's final job is to cut a joke.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Gag' looks like a joke; here it is the verb for heaving.
explanation.definitionFit: To gag is to heave as if about to vomit.

clue.text: This is oddly coloured

indicators.note: oddly means taking the letters in odd-numbered places

explanation.surface: A remark that something here is strangely tinted.
explanation.walkthrough: 'This' refers to the clue itself, the thing the solver is reading.
explanation.definitionFit: Self-reference: what you are reading is a crossword hint.

clue.text: Grouse when main road's used the wrong way — playing ball!

indicators.note: used the wrong way means the main road's letters are turned round where they sit

parts.note: a grouse is a complaint or gripe
the A1 is Britain's longest numbered road, written AI in crosswords

explanation.surface: Someone moans about a highway driven in reverse, then cheerily agrees to go along.
explanation.walkthrough: The A1 is the main road from London to Edinburgh; its letters AI in the grouse are turned to IA.
explanation.definitionFit: Playing ball is an idiom for cooperating, which is what an obliging person does.

clue.text: Audacious League of Nations enterprise originally unsupported

indicators.note: originally means taking the first letter of each of these words

explanation.surface: A historical bold venture of the League of Nations that nobody backed.
explanation.definitionFit: Being on one's own means having no helpers, i.e. without support.

clue.text: Here at sea might one see son strip off?

definitions.text: Here at sea might one see son strip off?

parts.words: Here at sea might one see son strip off?
parts.note: on a cruise ship people undress to sunbathe on an open top level; 'son' sounds like the sun they bask in

explanation.surface: A question about where on a ship a boy might undress.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Son' nods to the sun, and 'strip off' describes sunbathers on a ship's open level.
explanation.definitionFit: An open level of a ship set aside for sunbathing passengers.

clue.text: Bent journalist beyond suspicion

indicators.note: beyond places the journalist after the suspicion in the word

parts.note: a hunch is a suspicion or intuition
ED, short for editor, is a common crossword journalist

explanation.surface: A crooked reporter is above suspicion.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bent' suggests corrupt; here it means stooped.
explanation.definitionFit: A synonym: a back bent this way is stooped forward and bowed over.
